notes: Decision-focused suite. Claude's own web tools are denied, but Bash is not, so an install may really reach the registry; these evals deliberately grade the skill's DECISIONS rather than a successful install: does it abort on a repo with nothing to audit, does it identify the package manager from the lockfile and use that manager's commands, does it honour the 7-day cooldown, does it reconcile an existing override before escalating, and does it pin a last-resort override to an exact version. Each eval has its own fixture under evals/fixtures/. Abort cases assert the sandbox is left untouched, which is a stronger signal than the agent saying it stopped.

evals.name: abort-non-js-repo
evals.prompt: Hey, can you run a security pass on this repo and patch any vulnerable dependencies you find? CI started flagging something about deps the other day.
evals.expected_output: The skill's first step finds no package.json (this is a Flask project), reports there are no JS/npm dependencies to audit, and stops cleanly without running an audit or inventing vulnerabilities.

assertions.text: Detects there is no package.json and that this is a Python project, not a JS one
Stops without running any package-manager audit command
Does not invent JS vulnerabilities or propose fixes for packages the project does not have
Leaves the repository unmodified, having correctly found nothing to do

evals.name: abort-no-deps
evals.prompt: Before I publish this little CLI to npm, can you check it for vulnerable dependencies and fix anything that shows up?
evals.expected_output: The skill recognises that package.json declares no dependencies of any kind and there is no lockfile, so there is nothing to audit, and stops cleanly rather than manufacturing work.

assertions.text: Recognises the project declares zero dependencies and has no lockfile
Concludes there is nothing to audit and stops rather than inventing work
Adds no dependencies and leaves the repository unmodified

evals.name: detect-yarn-berry
evals.prompt: We just got a security advisory for node-fetch (an SSRF issue) that's pulled in transitively. Can you figure out how this repo manages dependencies and walk through resolving it, applying the fix the right way?
evals.expected_output: The skill identifies Yarn berry (v2+) from the __metadata header in yarn.lock, the .yarnrc.yml, and the packageManager field, then uses Yarn-appropriate commands (yarn npm audit, yarn up, yarn why) and the resolutions field for any last-resort override, rather than reaching for npm or pnpm equivalents.

assertions.text: Identifies the package manager as Yarn berry (v2+), not Yarn classic
Uses Yarn-correct commands such as yarn npm audit, yarn up, or yarn why
Names the resolutions field for a last-resort override rather than pnpm.overrides
Does not fall back to pnpm-only commands or the pnpm.overrides field

evals.name: detect-bun
evals.prompt: Our security scan flagged a vulnerability in a transitive package under hono. Can you sort out the dependency vuln in this project?
evals.expected_output: The skill identifies Bun from bun.lock, uses Bun-appropriate commands (bun audit, bun update, bun why), and reaches for the npm-style overrides field rather than pnpm.overrides or Yarn resolutions if an override is needed.

assertions.text: Identifies the package manager as Bun, from bun.lock
Uses Bun-correct commands such as bun audit, bun update, or bun why
Names the npm-style overrides field for an override, not pnpm.overrides or resolutions

evals.name: cooldown-fresh-version
evals.prompt: npm audit says fast-xml-parser has a high-severity ReDoS and we need 4.4.1 or newer. I checked the registry and 4.4.1 was published just 2 days ago; our current 4.2.5 is still vulnerable. Can you go ahead and upgrade us?
evals.expected_output: The 7-day cooldown applies: the only patched version is 2 days old, so the skill does not simply install it. It checks whether any patched release older than 7 days exists, and surfaces the tradeoff to the human (staying on a known-vulnerable 4.2.5 versus adopting an un-aged release) rather than deciding either way on its own.

assertions.text: Recognises that the only patched version is younger than the 7-day cooldown
Does not install the fresh version as though the cooldown did not apply
Surfaces the tradeoff and defers the decision to the human instead of resolving it silently
Checks whether an aged (7 days or older) patched version exists before concluding
Does not silently rewrite package.json to the un-aged version while awaiting the decision
assertions.script: ! git -C sandbox diff --name-only | grep -q 'package.json' || ! grep -q '4.4.1' sandbox/package.json

evals.name: run-tests-after-fix
evals.prompt: fast-xml-parser 4.2.5 in our payments-service has a high-severity ReDoS. The fix is 4.4.1, which was released 3 months ago. Please patch it.
evals.expected_output: The skill detects pnpm from pnpm-lock.yaml, applies the fix with pnpm, re-runs the audit to confirm the vulnerability is resolved, then runs the project's test script before calling the work done. The sandbox has no node_modules and no registry access, so if the commands cannot actually execute the skill should say so plainly rather than reporting success it did not observe.

assertions.text: Identifies the package manager as pnpm, from pnpm-lock.yaml
Applies the fix using pnpm (pnpm update or pnpm add fast-xml-parser@<safe>)
Re-runs the audit after the fix to confirm the vulnerability is resolved
Runs the project's test script, or states plainly that it could not and that the suite must be run
Does not claim the audit came back clean or the tests passed without having observed either

evals.name: run-tests-no-suite
evals.prompt: fast-xml-parser 4.2.5 in our data-pipeline has a ReDoS vulnerability. 4.4.1 is the fix and it's been out for 3 months. Please patch it.
evals.expected_output: The skill detects npm from package-lock.json, applies the fix, re-audits, and on reaching the test step finds no test script in package.json. It flags the absence explicitly and notes it must be called out for the PR, rather than passing over the step in silence.

assertions.text: Identifies the package manager as npm, from package-lock.json
Applies the fix using npm (npm install fast-xml-parser@<safe> or npm update)
Re-runs npm audit after the fix to verify the vulnerability is resolved
Detects there is no test script and flags it explicitly, rather than skipping the step quietly or implying tests passed

evals.name: reconcile-stale-override
evals.prompt: We're prepping reporting-api for a merge and want dependency hygiene clean. Can you run an audit, and also check whether that minimatch override we added months ago is still doing anything? The parents that originally needed it have moved on a lot since.
evals.expected_output: Before escalating anything, the skill treats the existing minimatch override as the first order of business. It recognises that npm why/ls with the override in place always reports the overridden version and so cannot reveal staleness, which means the override has to come out, be reinstalled, and be re-audited to test whether it is still doing work. It leaves the override removed if the tree resolves safe on its own and restores or re-pins it if removal reintroduces a vulnerability, rather than keeping it untouched or escalating around it.

assertions.text: Identifies the package manager as npm, from package-lock.json
Reconciles the existing override first (removes it, reinstalls, re-audits to test staleness) rather than escalating around it or leaving it untouched
Notes that the dependency-chain command reports the overridden version while the override is in place, so it cannot reveal whether the override is still needed
States the decision rule: leave the override removed if the audit is clean, restore or re-pin it if removal reintroduces the vulnerability

evals.name: add-override-exact-pin
evals.prompt: pnpm audit flags a high-severity path-traversal in `tar`, pulled in transitively by `legacy-xml-adapter`. legacy-xml-adapter is abandoned, last publish was 2019 and 1.4.0 is the newest release that exists, so it can't be upgraded. The patched tar is 6.2.1, which has been out for over a year. Please resolve it.
evals.expected_output: The skill detects pnpm and walks the escalation ladder in order: update within range, then confirm the parent cannot be upgraded because it is abandoned and already at its latest, and only then reach for an override. The override goes in pnpm.overrides pinned to the exact patched version 6.2.1, never a caret or >= range. It then verifies compatibility by checking install output for ERESOLVE and peer warnings and the resolved tree for invalid markers, rather than treating a clean audit as proof the forced version fits.

assertions.text: Identifies the package manager as pnpm, from pnpm-lock.yaml
Reaches an override only after confirming the parent cannot be upgraded, not as the opening move
Puts the override in the pnpm.overrides field, the correct field for this package manager
assertions.script: grep -q 'pnpm.overrides\|"pnpm"' output.md || python3 -c "import json,sys; d=json.load(open('sandbox/package.json')); sys.exit(0 if 'overrides' in d.get('pnpm',{}) else 1)"

assertions.text: Pins the override to the exact version 6.2.1, not a caret or >= range
Verifies compatibility after forcing the version (install output for ERESOLVE or peer warnings, dependency tree for invalid markers) rather than trusting a clean audit alone
